title: Japan announces new permanent residency guidelines, foreigners must earn more than average Japanese person
description: Japanese government suddenly raises income bar for foreigners seeking permanent residency, will apply new rules even to applications filed six months ago. On Thursday, the Japanese government announced new guidelines for foreigners seeking permanent residence in Japan. Under Japan’s Immigration Control Act, foreign nationals seeking to become permanent residents of Japan must satisfy three conditions. […]
content:
Japanese government suddenly raises income bar for foreigners seeking permanent residency, will apply new rules even to applications filed six months ago.

On Thursday, the Japanese government announced new guidelines for foreigners seeking permanent residence in Japan.

Under Japan’s Immigration Control Act, foreign nationals seeking to become permanent residents of Japan must satisfy three conditions. They must demonstrate good conduct (i.e. not break any laws) and have financial assets/job skills that will prevent them from becoming a burden on social welfare programs. Finally, the applicant’s permanent residency status must be determined to serve Japan’s national interests.

Those are all broadly defined conditons, and the Japanese government’s new interpretation of them is going to significantly raise the bar for displaying financial security. Until now, an annual income of roughly 3 million yen (US$19,000) was considered to be a baseline, but generally acceptable, amount for a permanent residency applicant. 3 million yen isn’t a lot; it’s more or less a typical salary for a low-level office job in Japan. Still, with proper budgeting and a frugal lifestyle, it’s enough to make ends meet.

Under the new guidelines, however, foreigners will have to show that they earn an annual income above the national average for Japanese citizens. It’s unclear whether this is referring to the applicant’s individual income or that of their household as a whole, but according to government statistics the average unmarked adult income in Japan is approximately 4.5 million yen, bringing minimum required income up by 50 percent. The increase is even larger if evaluators are going to be using the average household income for Japanese citizens, which is 5.8 million yen.

But hey, if those foreigners who want to obtain permanent residency status can’t pull themselves up by their bootstraps and double their income, they can just file their applications before the new guidelines go into effect, right? Nope. The government announced the new guidelines on October 1, and said that the higher-than-average-Japanese-citizen income requirement will be applied to permanent residence applications filed as of April, but that’s not April of next year. No, the new income guideline is being retroactively applied to applications that were submitted as much as six months ago.

▼ It seems unreasonable to make the only alternative to the retroactive increase be to travel back in time and file your application on an earlier date, seeing as how even the wealthy struggle to find usable time machines.

Two other criteria are set to change from this coming April, one of which involves the amount of time a foreigner who’s married to a Japanese citizen has to live in Japan before they can obtain permanent residency. Currently, the couple must have been married for at least three years, and the foreign spouse must have lived in Japan for at least one year in order to be eligible. From April, those requirements are going to be lengthened to the couple having been married for five years, and the foreign spouse having lived in Japan for at least three. Note that these requirements are in addition to the above income requirement, not a substitute for it.

Foreign residents who are not married to a Japanese citizen will need to have lived in Japan for 10 years in order to be eligible for permanent residency, an amount of time which is unchanged from the current system. The 10-year residency requirement is going to be a moot point for many younger applicants, though, because from April evaluators will also be looking at permanent residency applicants’ projected pension benefits, with the new guidelines saying applicants should have benefits equivalent to those of someone who has been paying into Japan’s national pension system for 30 years.

All of this is taking place against a backdrop of Japanese residents dealing with the most severe price inflation in generations for basic goods and services, while also seeing more and more foreign tourists spending carefreely while on vacation in Japan. At the same time, Japan’s foreign resident population has increased, but as the majority of them are working for Japanese employers and getting paid in yen, they’re not reaping the benefits of the weak yen that foreign tourists are. Foreign residents can still make easy scapegoats for frustrated Japanese nationals who feel like their standard of living is eroding, though, and with foreign residents of Japan not being able to vote, it’s not surprising that politicians going to bat for them on this matter are in short supply.

Aside from playing to the preferences of a certain segment of the voter base, it’s hard to see how the new guidelines will actually benefit Japan. The required 30 years of pension benefits is likely to have a negative affect on younger foreigner’ interest in relocating to Japan, since it would involve taking on the risk of potentially spending their prime working years in Japan without knowing whether they’ll be able to settle in the country permanently until they hit their 50s. That, in turn, lessens the potential for immigration to help counteract the negative effects of Japan’s falling birthrate and shrinking total population. Raising permanent residency requirements isn’t going to do anything to help Japan attract the world’s best and brightest expats, either. The stricter guidelines don’t do anything to benefit them, and between Japan’s lower salaries for executive positions compared to overseas companies, plus the weak yen, high-flying professionals can earn significantly more working elsewhere, then enjoy the best of what Japan has to offer to wealthy leisure tourists without really needing to reside in the country.

But hey, at least if foreign residents are unable to obtain permanent residency under the new guidelines, at least they can look forward to paying higher fees when they have to renew their visas.

Source: Mainichi Shimbun, Asahi Shimbun

title: Japanese scientists grow sheet of heart muscle cells for world’s first general-patient ReHeart-ing
description: Patient had a new piece of her own heart attached to her old one. We often report on scientific and medical breakthroughs that have the potential to change the world, but more often than not, they seem to just disappear. You may even remember back in 2006, when Shinya Yamanaka announced that he had converted […]
content:
Patient had a new piece of her own heart attached to her old one.

We often report on scientific and medical breakthroughs that have the potential to change the world, but more often than not, they seem to just disappear. You may even remember back in 2006, when Shinya Yamanaka announced that he had converted mature skin cells into pluripotent stem cells, cells which are capable of taking on any function. These induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells even won Yamanaka the Nobel Prize in 2012.

But after that, not much came of it outside of research labs, until 29 September, when the world’s first commercialized iPS treatment, ReHeart, took place at Osaka Police Hospital. ReHeart was developed by Osaka University Professor Emeritus Yoshiki Sawa and his biotech startup Cuorips and involves creating a sheet of heart muscle cells from iPS cells and applying it to the heart of a patient suffering from severe heart disease.

▼ ReHeart muscle sheets and a model of a functioning heart made from 200 million iPS cells were on display at the Osaka Expo last year.

The treatment was approved by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare with the condition that its efficacy is verified in the next seven years. Having been tested on eight people in the past, the first general patient was a woman in her 50s who suffered from severe heart failure after having a heart attack. The surgery took about 50 minutes, and no problems were reported.

Sawa acknowledged that 20 years was a long wait for the practical application of this medical discovery, but even that was only achieved through the hard work of medical professionals as well as the support of private companies and the government. He hopes things will be able to move forward more quickly from this point onward.

Readers of the news, however, expressed a great deal of impatience in online comments, especially when it comes to potential iPS treatments for their own personal afflictions.

“That’s great and all, but how about making some hair! HAIR!!!”
“We’ll need to create tooth, hair, and kidney regeneration next.”
“It’s only gotten this far?”
“When will we see the regeneration of optic nerve bundles and retinas?”
“I would like to have two more arms.”
“I wish they could make something that cures cold sores instantly.”
“I wish they had sheets of brain cells too.”
“Dr. Yamanaka… It’s time… to talk about hair.”
“Baldness isn’t life-threatening, so it’s on the back burner.”

Though iPS cells do have the potential to restore hair growth, the cost would probably be astronomical. Estimates for ReHeart are upwards of 15 million yen (US$96,000), but Japan’s national healthcare systems would only require a patient to pay about 30 percent of that, with further reductions made based on their age and income.

However, ReHeart is simply a sheet of uniform heart muscle cells, whereas recreating even a single hair follicle is considerably more complex, with multiple different types of cells working in unison. Also, since it’s not a life-threatening condition, insurance won’t cover hair-growth therapy, requiring the patient to pay the full amount. Needless to say, anyone seeking new hair this way will have to pay an arm and a leg, and then pay again for a new arm and leg generated by iPS cells.

On the bright side, another treatment that was approved alongside ReHeart was Amchepry, dopaminergic neural progenitor cells created from iPS cells and used to help restore motor function to patients with advanced Parkinson’s disease.

Seeing effective treatments for these two illnesses that inflict pain and suffering on millions of people around the world is encouraging, and better late than never.

Source: YTV News, Itai News, Cell & Gene Therapy Review

title: “We’d heard Japan’s sentences are light” say foreign travelers arrested for Tokyo robberies
description: Pair of thieves broke into house in Tokyo one day after arriving in Japan. On August 21, 24-year-old Chilean national Pinya Guzman and his 33-year-old countryman Mansano Quesad arrived at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport on a flight from Australia. The pair were quite busy for the next few days, pulling a smash-and-grab robbery in a luxury […]
content:
Pair of thieves broke into house in Tokyo one day after arriving in Japan.

On August 21, 24-year-old Chilean national Pinya Guzman and his 33-year-old countryman Mansano Quesad arrived at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport on a flight from Australia. The pair were quite busy for the next few days, pulling a smash-and-grab robbery in a luxury watch shop in Tokyo’s Nakano neighborhood on August 25, fleeing halfway across the country to Osaka, and then getting arrested in a vacation rental property on August 27.

It turns out, though, the pair started breaking the law even earlier than initially thought. During the investigation into their activities after arriving in Japan, the police were able to determine that on August 22, the very next day after they landed, the two men also broke into a house in Tokyo’s Ota Ward, where they stole three more luxury watches and seven other valuable items with a total value of approximately 7.9 million yen (US$50,000).

The men, who have admitted to the August 22 break-in, say that they had not chosen their burglary target prior to arriving in Japan. Instead, they saw they went to a wealthy part of Ota Ward and simply walked around until they saw someone getting in their car and driving away from a house. After they spotted someone doing that at around 11:35 in the morning, they waited for the car to drive out of sight, then rang the house’s doorbell. When no one answered, they broke one of the house’s windows and Guzman acted as a lookout while Quesad entered the home and stole the watches, other items, and around 200 Euros in cash that he came across.

In explaining the motivation for such an unplanned, breezy burglary, Quesad told the police:

“We’d heard back in Chile that sentences are light in Japan, so we went looking for a house to rob in a rich neighborhood.”

The thieves say that they planned to sell some of their stolen goods to a fence in Italy who they know from previous thefts they committed in Europe. Investigators were also able to determine that airline ticket data had been sent to the pair’s smartphones for a departure from Osaka’s International Airport on the day they were arrested, with their scheduled route taking them through Italy on their way back to Chile.

As for whether or not Japan is soft on crime, theft alone can carry a sentence of up to 10 years imprisonment, so it’s not like prosecutors are limited to doling out feckless slaps on the wrist. And in a broader sense of societal attitudes about criminal justice, while it’s not something that would be applied to property theft, the death penalty does exist in Japan, and unlike in Chile, it’s not reserved for extraordinary circumstances like treason or war crimes.

In addition, under Japan’s rearrest system, the Chilean pair, who were already in jail in Osaka, have now been rearrested for the home break-in, thus resetting the 23 days they can remain locked up before they even have to be formally arraigned. And since the burglary contains multiple potential charges (theft, property damage, and trespassing, to name just three), the time limit for their pre-arraignment incarceration could be reset a few more times too.

The two men (or whoever they got their info from) may have had the idea that the Japanese legal system is lenient on crimes committed by foreigners, which was, in a sense, true for many years. For quite some time, when foreigners in Japan got in trouble with the law, a speedy deportation was often the end result. However, this pattern existed in a time when foreigner-committed crimes in Japan tended to be predominantly things like a drunken bar scuffle, minor vandalism, or petty shoplifting, situations where things could be smoothed over by paying for repairs and an assurance that the perpetrator wouldn’t come back again. A multimillion-yen robbery, though, is something on a much higher level of heinousness, and a home break-in introduces the possibility of physical danger to anyone who might have been in the house or returned to it while the burglary was going on. Those aren’t the sort of things Japan is willing to just shrug its shoulders and say “Can’t be helped” over, especially with foreigner-committed crimes growing more frequent and larger in scale, causing many to worry that local laws and social norms aren’t being respected by visitors from overseas.

title: Foreign sports team competing in Japan finds critical uniform item at convenience store
description: Family Mart proves once again that Japanese convenience stores have everything. No matter how well-packed you think you are when traveling overseas, there’s always the chance that it won’t be until after you arrive that you find out there’s something else you should have brought with you. That was the situation Uzbekistan’s men’s volleyball team […]
content:
Family Mart proves once again that Japanese convenience stores have everything.

No matter how well-packed you think you are when traveling overseas, there’s always the chance that it won’t be until after you arrive that you find out there’s something else you should have brought with you. That was the situation Uzbekistan’s men’s volleyball team found itself in when they reached Nagoya prior to their opening match in the currently ongoing 2026 Asian Games, and discovered that they needed socks.

The problem wasn’t that no one on the team had packed socks, but that different members of the team had packed different kinds. It turns out that the Asian Games’ uniforms regulations include a clause that all players must wear socks with a color, length, and pattern that matches their teammates’.

They needed to address the situation as quickly as possible, but when the team took the court for their opening match against Japan on September 27, not only did the Uzbekistani players’ socks match each other, they also featured the blue, white, and green color scheme of their country’s flag.

▼ September 27 match between Uzbekistan and Japan

▼ Flag of Uzbekistan

So did the Uzbekistani team arrange for an overnight air shipment of socks from home? Did they manage to find an all-night textile mill and arrange for a customized rush order?

Nope. They just did what anybody’s first move should be when you suddenly need something in Japan: they went shopping at a Japanese convenience store. Luckily, there happened to be one right by the hotel they were staying out, and even more luckily, it was a branch of Family Mart…

…and yet more luckily still, Family Mart just so happens to sell socks with stirpes in the chain’s image colors, which are also blue, white, and green!

Even that wasn’t the full extent of the team’s luck, because in addition to their appropriate aesthetics, Family Mart’s socks are known for their high quality. In recent years, Family Mart has been elevating its apparel items beyond something that you’d only wear in an emergency, with its Convenience Wear line getting thumbs up from satisfied customers for its comfort and durability. The socks in question are officially called the Line Socks Combini White and are priced at 429 yen (US$2.70) a pair, so they didn’t even put much of a dent in the team’s travel expenses.

▼ We’re fans ourselves.

Japan loves watching its teams compete in international sporting events, and TV viewers were happy to see Japan win the September 27 match in straight sets, but many also couldn’t take their eyes off the Uzbekistani team’s socks and wonder about the possible convenience store connection. In an interview, two players later confirmed that they had indeed sourced that part of their uniforms from Family Mart, and the company has said that it’s happy to have been of assistance on such a major stage as the sporting event.

Maybe this sudden surge in interest for Family Mart’s image-color socks will lead the chain to reissue its mini socks for use on ice cream containers, but even if they don’t, their new line of socks representing all 47 prefectures of Japan still gives lots of options to choose from.

Source: Mainichi Shimbun (1, 2), The Digest, Asian Games, Family Mart

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Pumpkin Soupuccino for autumn
description: Blurring the line between soup and cappuccino for Japan’s colder days.  Two years ago, Starbucks Japan hard-launched a new product called the Soupuccino, which reimagines the cappuccino by replacing the coffee with soup. Now, the Soupuccino is returning to keep us feeling warm and cosy this autumn, and this time it features the flavour of […]
content:
Blurring the line between soup and cappuccino for Japan’s colder days. 

Two years ago, Starbucks Japan hard-launched a new product called the Soupuccino, which reimagines the cappuccino by replacing the coffee with soup. Now, the Soupuccino is returning to keep us feeling warm and cosy this autumn, and this time it features the flavour of pumpkin, to capture the taste of the season.

▼ This warm and frothy pumpkin soup is topped with the kind of airy foam you’d normally expect to find on a cappuccino.

Made with pumpkins sourced from the famous pumpkin-growing region of Hokkaido, the soup also contains onion, celery, black pepper and nutmeg for added depth of flavour. A hint of maple flavouring brings out the natural sweetness of the pumpkin, while milk gives the soup a mellow richness.

According to Starbucks, the chain’s baristas froth up each serving individually, creating a light, fluffy foam that gives the soup its cappuccino-like texture. As you make your way through the beverage, the texture gradually becomes thicker and creamier, while the pumpkin’s sweetness becomes more pronounced.

▼ The Pumpkin Soupuccino is available in Short and Tall sizes, priced at 500 yen (US$3.17) and 540 yen respectively for dine-in, or 491 and 530 yen for takeout.

Just as they might do with a cappuccino, customers can customise the soup by changing the milk component – soy milk is available at no extra charge and other milk options can be selected for an additional 55 yen.

If you’re feeling peckish, Starbucks has you covered with its recently revamped baguettes, giving us four new varieties made with a high-hydration dough to give them a moister, softer mouthfeel.

▼ Clockwise from top left: Ham & Gouda (530 yen takeout, 540 yen dine-in), Two Kinds of Chocolate & Butter (510 yen/520 yen), Three Kinds of Mushrooms and Roast Chicken (628 yen/640 yen), Herb Sausage (648 yen/660 yen).

According to Starbucks, the mushroom and chocolate and butter baguettes are seasonal specials for autumn, while the sausage and ham & gouda varieties will be mainstays on the menu.

A baguette and a frothy Soupuccino sounds like the perfect autumn meal for Japan’s colder days, and the seasonal offerings will be on the menu for a limited time from 30 September.

title: Sample lots of little Japanese dishes at this hidden all-you-can-eat lunch buffet in Shinjuku
description: Want to try all kinds of Japanese dishes but don’t know where to start? This gem with “hidden” in its name has got you covered.  Just recently we learned of a restaurant in Tokyo’s bustling Shinjuku district where you can sample over 35 kinds of Japanese dishes at an all-you-can-eat lunch buffet. Kakurebo (literally, “Hidden […]
content:
Want to try all kinds of Japanese dishes but don’t know where to start? This gem with “hidden” in its name has got you covered. 

Just recently we learned of a restaurant in Tokyo’s bustling Shinjuku district where you can sample over 35 kinds of Japanese dishes at an all-you-can-eat lunch buffet. Kakurebo (literally, “Hidden Room”) is on the 7th floor of the Adhoc Building in Shinjuku’s Sanchome district, less than a 10-minute walk from our editorial offices. It so lived up to its name, in fact, that it had escaped the notice of even our veteran writers who have been working in the neighborhood for over 20 years.

▼ A sign for the restaurant with “hidden” (隠れ) in its name outside of the building

 

We took the elevator up and were greeted by a multilingual sign inviting us inside.

Details about the lunch buffet were front and center. 90 minutes of all-you-can-eat dishes and a drink bar for 1,800 yen (US$11.45) for adults/600 yen for kids (ages 6-12) on weekdays and 2,200 yen for adults/900 yen for kids on weekends didn’t seem like a bad deal. Children under six are free.

We’d heard rumors that there are sometimes lines around lunch time, but it was fairly calm on this particular day when we stopped by around 12:15 p.m.

Not only did we see Japanese-style dishes everywhere, but there was also an assortment of cold Chinese-style vegetable sides and other kinds of side dishes.

Hot dishes included ebi shinjo (minced shrimp and seafood dumplings), simmered root vegetables, stir-fried veggies, and stuffed cabbage.

We had assumed that a restaurant specializing in Japanese dishes might lean on the healthy side of things, but there plenty of deep-fried Western-style Japanese dishes as well such as chicken karaage and pork skewers, plus French fries.

The chicken, shrimp, and sweet potato tempura offerings were especially enticing.

For those who need rice to ground themselves, never fear, because there was plenty of white rice and a multigrain rice blend as well. Somewhat unusually, there was also pollack roe udon.

Our first spread looked like this. It was perfect for trying a little bit of a lot of things.

Thankfully, the taste of everything was generally excellent. All of the dishes were seasoned well and at an appropriate level for lunch, whether it was the eggplant stew or the tofu hamburg.

Overall there seemed to be a lot of chicken-based dishes, but there were so many different takes and styles of preparation that we never got bored.

Even if we did, we could always spice things up with some salt, curry salt, matcha salt, or yukari (shiso) salt in the seasonings corner.

Our only potential gripe was that the udon noodles were a bit on the soft side, but the pollack roe accents made up for it in a burst of flavor.

The curry also held a subtle dashi flavor befitting of Japanese-style cuisine that made it pair well with the other dishes as well.

For dessert, we had a few cubes of coffee jelly, almond jelly, and a sliced waffle to round off our meal. All of those little bites sure added up!

Finally, regarding the vibes, we thought the interior of the restaurant was spacious, clean, and modern-looking. We’ll definitely be going back–especially on days when we need to escape the craziness of the office!

It seems that Shinjuku Sanchome will never stop surprising us with delicious places that have been right under our noses the whole time.

Restaurant information

title: Toys R Us is leaving Japan after 35 years in the country
description: U.S. born chain has soldiered on for nearly a decade after the closing of stores in America. Every now and then, U.S. companies that set up stores in Japan become so successful that they outlive their home-country selves. Mister Donut and convenience store Lawson, for example, both began in the States but have now been […]
content:
U.S. born chain has soldiered on for nearly a decade after the closing of stores in America.

Every now and then, U.S. companies that set up stores in Japan become so successful that they outlive their home-country selves. Mister Donut and convenience store Lawson, for example, both began in the States but have now been defunct there for so long that most people assume they originated in Japan. Similarly, you won’t find Barneys New York in New York anymore, or anywhere else in America, but there are still two branches of the luxury fashion retailer in Tokyo, plus three more in other Japanese cities.

For the past nine years, Toys R Us has been part of this category too. Even after the chain closed its last U.S. branch in 2017, Toys R Us Japan kept chugging along. Sadly, though, the company has finally reached its limit, and says that it will be leaving the Japanese market.

The decision comes after extended operating losses, with analysts pointing to two trends moving in opposite directions as the primary reason. Despite a recent bump, Japan’s birthrate has fallen dramatically, and with Toys R Us focusing primarily on toys for younger children (as opposed to, say, high-end anime collectibles), there’s far less total demand for the types of items they sell than there used to be. Meanwhile, online shopping continues to rise in popularity in Japan, so when the parents of young kids that the country does have are looking to buy toys, they’re not necessarily interested in visiting the large-scale physical stores that are the core of Toys R Us’ business model. Even when families are going out for shopping, Toys R Us has to compete with electronics retailers like Yodobashi Camera and Bic Camera, which often have toy sections of their own and can afford more conveniently central locations by nature of their broader and higher-margin product lineups.

▼ Toys R Us Japan uses the chain’s iconic commercial jingle, but with Japanese lyrics. For added bittersweet nostalgia, note the PlayStation 2 selling for 19,799 yen, compared to the 54,000 yen that PlayStation 5s start at.

Toys R Us Japan leaving the Japanese market isn’t going to be a minor shakeup. Since arriving in the country in 1991, it’s grown to approximately 150 stores across the country and currently employs a total of around 6,000 full and part-time workers. Thankfully, rather than the company being liquidated, it’s expected that Toys R Us Japan’s operations, physical assets, and staff will be acquired by Pan Pacific International Holdings. Though Pan Pacific doesn’t have a dedicated toy store chain of its own, it is the parent company of discount retailer Don Quijote, which sells just about everything imaginable, so there’s the potential to retain/retrain staff even after the Toys R Us brand is no more, but Pan Pacific itself is yet to publicly comment on the deal.

Source: Kyodo via Yahoo! Japan News, Yomiuri Shimbun

title: Starbucks Japan releases new Pikachu Honey Cream Latte into the wild for new Pokémon collaboration
description: We catch Pikachu at Starbucks and receive an exclusive sticker, but how does the electric Pokémon taste? Attention trainers! The Pokémon + Starbucks collaboration has begun!!! This dream collaboration stopped us in our tracks when it was announced last week, and though it sounded too good to be true, when we turned up at our […]
content:
We catch Pikachu at Starbucks and receive an exclusive sticker, but how does the electric Pokémon taste?

Attention trainers! The Pokémon + Starbucks collaboration has begun!!!

This dream collaboration stopped us in our tracks when it was announced last week, and though it sounded too good to be true, when we turned up at our nearest Starbucks on release day on 30 September, the star drink was there on the menu, waiting for us to catch it…so that’s exactly what we did.

Called the Pikachu Honey Cream Latte (690 yen [US$4.55] for dine-in), this limited-edition creation is made with milk and espresso, but unlike a regular latte, the espresso shot is poured in from the top to help create a visual that conjures up the colours of Pikachu.

There’s a lot to love about this rare drink, starting from the fact that it was chosen from more than 700 Pokémon-themed beverage recipes created by baristas from across Japan, as part of the “Pokémon + Starbucks Barista Battle”.

▼ Kind of like the work of a Pokémon Master, with the skills of a coffee master thrown in.

Image: Press release

Then there’s the look of the latte, with honey and caramel sauce giving the drink a Pikachu-like hue, while heart-shaped sugar pieces on top of the chocolate sauce-slathered honey-flavoured whipped cream are designed to mimic the red colour of Pikachu’s cheeks.

The latte was so beautifully crafted that we found it difficult to bring ourselves to drink it, but our curiosity about Pikachu’s taste got the better of us, so we dipped our straw in and took a sip.

First, we tried it as it was, without mixing it whatsoever, and it tasted like a familiar Starbucks latte, but noticeably sweeter. We expected the caramel to be more dominant, but instead the honey really packed a punch, imparting a sweet zap that reminded us of Pikachu.

After mixing the whipped cream and toppings into the drink, the flavour became richer and creamier, with a mellow aftertaste. The honey-flavoured whipped cream had a smooth, rich flavour reminiscent of custard, adding even more depth of flavour to the mix, and though we thought the flavours might battle with the chocolate, it turned out to be a perfect partnership. Everything came together beautifully, with the richness of espresso playing a faint melody in the background, while the heart-shaped sugar pieces provided an exciting crunchy textural accent right to the very end.

Though it ran sweeter than a regular latte, the Pikachu Honey Cream Latte left us completely satisfied. It delivered a sense of excitement and adventure, which is what you want on an outing with Pikachu, and the sticker we received free with purchase gave us a lasting memory of our journey together.

▼ The sticker illustration features an original design by illustrator Hikaru Ichijo, depicting Pikachu and a trainer, or rather, a barista, with a coffee.

▼ You can even purchase a Starbucks gift card with exclusive Pokémon + Starbucks collaboration artwork for a limited time.

The only downside to the Pikachu Honey Cream Latte is that, like any good adventure, it’s destined to end all too soon. The latte is only on the menu for 9 short days, until 8 October, so you’ll want to get in quick to join the journey, and be sure to catch all the Pokémon + Starbucks merchandise available exclusively online too.

title: To stir, or not to stir – A Japanese rice cooker debate
description: Rice cooker manufacturer weighs in on the question of whether you should stir your cooked rice before you scoop it out of the pot. Ideally, a rice cooker should take all of the guesswork out of making rice. Sure, if you want to get fancy you can fiddle around with fine-tuned settings, but in general […]
content:
Rice cooker manufacturer weighs in on the question of whether you should stir your cooked rice before you scoop it out of the pot.

Ideally, a rice cooker should take all of the guesswork out of making rice. Sure, if you want to get fancy you can fiddle around with fine-tuned settings, but in general you’re supposed to be able to put the rice and water in the pot, close the lid, hit the start button, and have a pot of completely acceptable rice ready to eat a little over half an hour later, right?

Ah, but even after the cooking cycle is done, there’s one more step before you can eat the rice, and it’s one that recently sparked a debate among Japanese Internet users: Should you stir the rice before you scoop it out of the pot?

The simplest thing to do when the rice is ready is simply to grab a rice scoop and scoop the amount you want to eat into your bowl or onto your plate. However, some foodies see this as at least a culinary faux pax, and potentially a way to ruin the remaining rice, and insist that before actually scooping any rice out first, the cooked grains need to be mixed.

炊き立てご飯を混ぜないで、こういうよそい方をする人は、廊下に立っててください pic.twitter.com/HSscvShmK1

— やまさん (@ikujidays) September 23, 2026

The above tweet, from a pro-mixing advocate showing a photo example of what not to do, brought nods of agreement from those saying that leaving the rice unmixed will also make its texture worse, even if it was cooked properly. And while some might be tempted to scoff at that as a pretentious attempt at putting on airs and assuming that the easy way of doing anything must also be the low-quality way of doing it, there actually is a scientific foundation for their stance, according to Tiger, one of Japan’s leading rice cooker manufacturers, Tiger.

On its website, Tiger explains that at the time that when the cooking cycle finishes, it leaves an excessive amount of moisture on the outer/upper surface of the rice inside the pot. If left to sit as-is, the outer layer will become soggy, which will then cause it to stick to the grains underneath it, resulting in clumps that harden. So if you want your rice to be as soft and fluffy as possible. Tiger says you’ve got to stir it as soon as you can after it’s done cooking.

Tiger even explains its recommended stirring technique. Using the edge of a rice scoop, carve a plus sign into the top of the rice. You don’t want to smash or squash the grains together, so instead of pressing down from above, slide the scoop into one of the grooves you’ve made and gently lift the rice up from the bottom, and from the inside of the pot towards the outer edge. Doing this will more evenly distribute the excess moisture that had accumulated along the outer edge and give you a more uniform, classically fluffy texture.

That said, the fact that Tiger felt the need to address the topic on its website demonstrates that not everyone in Japan is aware of how stirring the rice affects its texture, and even then there’s the question of how significant the difference is. Thought not the norm among people in Japan, a handful of commenters on the above tweet mentioned that they actually kind of prefer the harder texture that comes from not stirring the cooked rice, and a few also said that they didn’t feel like stirring provided enough of a texture improvement for them to actually make a habit of doing it every time they cook a pot. There were also a few commenters who pointed out that not stirring the rice inside the pot keeps the uneaten portion in a nicely defined block that’s easier to cover in plastic wrap and freeze to be eaten on a later date, so they were OK with the texture tradeoff. Still, if you’re going for the most authentic/orthodox Japanese rice experience, stirring the rice is the way to go.

Source: Tiger, Hachima Kiko

title: Foreign tourists get free Shinkansen tickets in Japan, and here’s how to claim them
description: Enjoy a free bullet train ride to one of the country’s most beautiful regions. International visitors to Japan tend to arrive and stay on the mainland, travelling between big cities like Tokyo and Kyoto on the Shinkansen bullet train. However, there are three other main islands in Japan crying out for tourists, and now one […]
content:
Enjoy a free bullet train ride to one of the country’s most beautiful regions.

International visitors to Japan tend to arrive and stay on the mainland, travelling between big cities like Tokyo and Kyoto on the Shinkansen bullet train. However, there are three other main islands in Japan crying out for tourists, and now one prefecture at the tip of Kyushu, the southernmost main island, is enticing tourists to visit by giving away free Shinkansen tickets.

The campaign is being offered by Kagoshima Prefecture, in partnership with travel booking platform Klook. Designed to encourage more international visitors to make the trip down to the southern end of Kyushu, the campaign comes with the following terms and conditions.

1. Travellers need to arrive in Japan via Fukuoka Airport and book at least one night at a participating hotel in Kagoshima Prefecture through Klook.
2. The campaign is currently open to travellers from the U.S., Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China.

If you fit those two requirements – congratulations! You’re eligible for a free one-way Shinkansen journey from Hakata to Kagoshima.

▼ The journey from Hakata to Kagoshima.

To receive the offer, first get your promo code on the Klook website and then book one of the Kagoshima hotel listings that show the “Receive Free Shinkansen Ticket” promotion. Once booked, enter your code at checkout, then fill out a short survey and you’ll get a code to redeem a one-way Shinkansen fare from Hakata to Kagoshima, up to the cost of 11,420 yen (US$72).

With Kagoshima being home to Sakurajima, one of the world’s most active volcanoes, as well as the UNESCO World Natural Heritage islands of Yakushima, Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima, there’s plenty to see and do in the area. The prefecture is also famous for its natural sand baths, Kagoshima Wagyu and black pork, amongst other local specialties.

According to Klook, the campaign aims to increase the number of visitors to Kagoshima, as many international visitors stop in Fukuoka without venturing further south, despite Kagoshima being two hours away by Shinkansen. The prefecture has allocated around 278 million yen (roughly $1.8 million) to subsidise the promotion, which is scheduled to run from 18 September to 28 February, while allocations remain available.

While the campaign represents a considerable saving, local reports suggest it remains relatively unknown by overseas tourists. Shortly after the campaign began, interviews at Kagoshima-Chuo Station revealed some international visitors were unaware of the offer, while others were taking advantage of different deals, like the 25,000-yen seven-day pass that gives you unlimited travel around Kyushu.

▼ The JR Kyushu Rail Pass is another great deal, and can be purchased here.

You could always get the free Shinkansen deal through Klook and then purchase one of the rail passes to discover more of what the island has to offer. With some of Japan’s best hot springs, and giant sushi on the luggage carousel at one of the local airports, Kyushu is a hidden gem that deserves to be on your radar, especially now that you can get a free Shinkansen ticket to travel there.
